options: Creates a new reference to a value
Follows a reference to reach the value it points at
Frees the memory a reference points at
quiz.explain: `*` dereferences: it follows the reference (signpost) back to the actual value. `&` makes a reference; `*` follows one — they are opposites.

quiz.q: Given `let r = &x;` where x is an i32, why does `r + 1` fail but `*r + 1` work?
options: `r` is a reference, not a number; `*r` gets the number so + works
`r + 1` works fine, the question is wrong
You must always write `&` before arithmetic
`*r` copies x into a new variable named r
quiz.explain: `r` is a `&i32` (a signpost), and you can't add 1 to a signpost. `*r` follows it to the actual number, then + 1 works.

quiz.q: Why can you call `r.len()` without writing `*` when r is a `&String`?
options: String has a special no-deref rule
The dot operator auto-follows references (deref coercion)
len() secretly takes a reference to a reference
It doesn't work; you must write (*r).len()
quiz.explain: The `.` operator automatically follows references as needed to find the method, so method calls rarely need an explicit `*`.

quiz.q: How do you add 1 to the value that a `&mut` reference `r` points at?
quiz.explain: `*r` follows the mutable reference to the real value, and `+= 1` changes it there. Without `*`, you'd try to change the signpost itself.

flashcards.front: What is a reference, in one image?
flashcards.back: A signpost: it points at a value stored elsewhere. It doesn't contain the value itself. You make one with `&`.
Follows a reference back to the value it points at. `&` creates a reference; `*` follows it. They're opposites.

flashcards.front: When do you need `*` and when not?
flashcards.back: Need it for arithmetic and assignment through a reference (`*r + 1`, `*r = 5`). Not for method calls — the dot operator auto-follows references.
A `&str` is a lightweight borrowed view of text. Thanks to deref coercion, a `&String` can be used where a `&str` is expected.
